stem: A wire carrying a current lies between the poles of a magnet, at right angles to the field. What happens?

options.content: It feels a force and moves.

options.rationale: There is a force on it.

explanation: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force (the motor effect).

stem: Which change reverses the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?

options.rationale: This makes the force bigger, not reversed.

options.content: Reversing both the current and the field

explanation: Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged.

stem: If both the current and the magnetic field are reversed, the force on the wire is reversed.
explanation: Reversing both quantities leaves the force in its original direction.

stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the first finger represent?

options.content: The magnetic field, from N to S

explanation: First finger: Field. seCond finger: Current. thuMb: Motion (force).

stem: A wire on a page carries a current from left to right. A magnetic field points into the page. In which direction is the force on the wire?

options.content: Towards the bottom of the page
options.rationale: Check the rule again: first finger into the page, second finger to the right.

options.content: Towards the top of the page

options.rationale: The force is at right angles to the field.
The force is at right angles to the field.

explanation: First finger into the page (field), second finger to the right (current): the thumb points to the top of the page.
hints: Use your left hand: first finger = field, second finger = current.

stem: A wire carries a current out of the page. A north pole is above the wire and a south pole below it. In which direction is the force on the wire?

options.rationale: Check the rule: field downwards, current out of the page.
The force is at right angles to the field.
The force is at right angles to the field.

explanation: Field from N to S points down; current out of the page. With the left hand, the thumb points to the right.
hints: The field points from the north pole to the south pole.

stem: When is there no force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?

options.content: When the current is at right angles to the field
When the current is parallel to the field lines
When the magnet is very strong
When the wire is made of copper

explanation: There is no force when the current flows along the field lines.

stem: A beam of electrons travels towards the top of a page through a magnetic field directed into the page. In which direction is the beam deflected?

options.rationale: Remember the conventional current is opposite to the electrons' motion.

options.content: Towards the bottom of the page

explanation: The conventional current points down the page (opposite to the electrons). First finger into the page, second finger down: the thumb points to the right.
hints: For electrons, point your second finger opposite to their motion.

stem: A beam of protons (positive particles) moves to the right through a magnetic field directed out of the page. In which direction are they deflected?
explanation: For positive particles the current is in their direction of motion. First finger out of the page, second finger to the right: the thumb points down.
hints: For positive particles, the current is in the direction they move.

stem: Why does a beam of charged particles move in a curve in a magnetic field?

options.content: The field slows the particles down as they move.
options.rationale: A magnetic force at right angles does not change their speed.

options.content: Gravity pulls them down into a curved path.
The force on them is always at right angles to their motion.
The particles become heavier in the magnetic field.

explanation: A force always at right angles to the motion changes its direction continuously, giving a circular path.

stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. What happens?

options.content: There is no force between them.
options.rationale: Each wire is in the other's field.

explanation: Parallel currents in the same direction attract; in opposite directions they repel.

stem: Two parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. Which explanation of the force between them is correct?

options.content: Between the wires their fields cancel, so the wires attract.
options.rationale: That happens for currents in the same direction.

options.content: There is no field in the gap between the wires.
options.rationale: Each wire has a field around it.

options.content: Between the wires the fields add, so the wires are pushed apart.
The fields cancel everywhere, so there is no force.
options.rationale: They do not cancel everywhere; each wire has its own field.

explanation: With opposite currents, the circular fields point the same way between the wires, so the field there is strong and the wires are pushed apart.
hints: Use the grip rule to find each wire's field in the region between them.

stem: Select **all** the changes that increase the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.

options.content: Turning the wire to lie along the field lines
options.rationale: This reduces the force to zero.
This reverses the force without making it bigger.

options.content: Increasing the length of wire in the field
Using a higher-resistance wire with the same p.d.
options.rationale: The current, and so the force, would be smaller.

explanation: The force grows with the current, the field strength and the length of wire in the field.
hints: Reversing something changes the direction, not the size.

stem: A learner rests a light copper rod across two horizontal copper rails that pass between the poles of a U-shaped magnet. The rails are connected to a battery and a switch.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: When the switch is closed, the rod rolls along the rails. Why?

options.content: The rod is magnetised and attracted to the magnet.
The current heats the rod and it expands along the rails.
Static charge on the rails pushes the rod along.
options.rationale: The rails are connected to a supply, not charged statically.

options.content: It carries a current in a magnetic field, so a force acts on it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State two different ways of making the rod roll the other way.

points.description: Reverse the current (swap the battery connections)
Reverse the magnetic field (turn the magnet over)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The learner reverses both the battery and the magnet. Which way does the rod roll?

options.rationale: Only one reversal would do that.

options.content: It rolls in the original direction, but faster
options.rationale: The size of the force is unchanged.

parts.explanation: Reversing both the current and the field leaves the force unchanged.

explanation: A current in a magnetic field feels a force; reversing one of current or field reverses it, reversing both does not.
hints: Copper is not magnetic: the force comes from the current.
